Our Sun knows how to get in the spirit! 🎃 Years ago, our Solar Dynamics Observatory caught our Sun looking like a jack-o’-lantern, with active regions shaped like a carved face. Swipe to see other cosmic curiosities captured over the years. #NASA #Halloween #Space The wispy white gas of this star-forming cloud, Lupus 3, is 500 light-years away in the constellation Scorpius. It looks something like a wave of ectoplasm or stretch of cobwebs. Which do you see? As we set our sights on the Hourglass Nebula, it appears to gaze back at us. This creepy cosmic object is a planetary nebula, the glowing relic of a dying, Sun-like star. This ghoulish cloud of gas and dust, called the Ghost Nebula, is 550 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia. Its long ghostly veil is shaped by radiation from the bright stars embedded within it. This witch is busy brewing baby stars! Named the Witch Head, this nebula is found 800 light-years away in the constellation Orion, just off the hunter’s “knee.”

Halloween is a time for things that go bump in the night. National parks have plenty of those. Boo! Still with us? From mysterious noises in the woods to wildlife that would prefer you keep your distance, the great outdoors can be downright spooky after dark. But the scariest encounters often have less to do with ghosts and more to do with poor planning, questionable decisions, and the occasional tree root working in cahoots with gravity. Whether you’re hiking a shadowy trail, camping beneath a full moon, or simply enjoying the autumn scenery, a few simple precautions can help keep your adventure from becoming a horror story. Stay on marked trails, watch your step, give wildlife plenty of space, check the weather, and pack the essentials. And if something in the woods starts whispering your name? Well, perhaps don’t investigate. Good luck! NPS

This spooky season, we're bringing you a tale of Halloween botany! The story begins with a dedicated search for the extremely rare and globally-vulnerable St. Lawrence grapefern (Sceptridium rugulosum). After weeks of combing potential habitat, one of our botanists was rewarded by finding this plant in a unique location — at the foot of a grave in a sandy cemetery in the Champlain Valley! While the location of this find is seasonally apropos, this is an exciting discovery for a more important reason: since the 90s, this species has been on the decline in Vermont. This find represents the first new population in Vermont in around 30 years, and this cemetery is currently the only known site for this rare grapefern in New England! Cemeteries often contain interesting plants that thrive in the low-competition environments created by consistent mowing as well as easy-to-dig-in sandy substrates. We’re not kitten around! @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb captured a purr-fect view of the Cat’s Head Nebula. This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. These clips of a Map Turtle hatchling emerging and being released into the Missisquoi Bay were captured by our biologists as they carried out turtle nest excavation last week at Sandy Point in Swanton. Turtle nests are carefully excavated for two main reasons: the first is so that we can document the number of successful nests and hatchlings produced, and the second is to protect live young still in the ground from being eaten by predators. The threatened Eastern Spiny Softshell Turtle is the target species in this work, and three sites are managed for their nesting, with Sandy Point being historically the most important; however, other turtle species use the same beach, including Painted Turtles, Common Snapping Turtles, and Map Turtles, like the one seen here.

Bats have a remarkable ability called echolocation, which allows them to navigate in the dark by making high-pitched sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back. Essentially, they shout into the void and wait for the void to explain where everything is. Same. Still waiting… These sound waves help bats locate insects, avoid obstacles, and navigate their surroundings with impressive accuracy. They can even detect objects as small as human hair. Meanwhile, some humans have been known to walk into a glass door in broad daylight. One time. Moving on. Bats are an important part of many national park ecosystems, helping control insect populations and keeping nature ticking along after dark. So, the next time you hear a bat making noises, remember it isn’t screaming into the darkness. Well, it is, but it’s using a highly sophisticated biological sonar system. Screaming with purpose. Try it. Watch out for that door. NPS Photos: Bats flying in the darkness

We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! THE hottest color of the season is hunter orange! Not only does fluorescent orange make a chic fashion statement, but more importantly, it keeps hunters and all outdoor recreators visible to other people in the woods. Wearing a hunter orange hat or vest is important for everyone in the woods during hunting season. Whether you're hunting, bird watching, or trail running, bright orange can help you be seen, even in low-light. While it isn’t recommended to wear orange during waterfowl and turkey seasons, we do still suggest folks chasing fall ducks, geese and turkey wear hunter orange when going to and from blind tree stands or calling spots. Same goes for bowhunters walking up to their treestands or climbing down at the end of the day. Be smart and safe outdoors this fall. Wear orange!

These ocean habitats face many pressures, and how seafood is caught and farmed is one of them.
